questions.title: Liver resection when extrahepatic disease is treated or treatable
questions.question: When colorectal cancer has extrahepatic disease that is treated or completely treatable, when should liver resection be offered?
questions.proposal: Treated or completely treatable extrahepatic disease is not an absolute contraindication to curative-intent liver resection, but complete clearance of every site is mandatory and benefit depends on the site. Lung disease has the best outcome; nodal disease does poorly (pooled 5-year survival about 15%), worst beyond the hepatic pedicle; limited peritoneal disease belongs to expert CRS/HIPEC centres. Any extrahepatic disease ends transplant intent (CRLM-B5).
rules: Lung: combined or staged liver and lung metastasectomy after joint HPB–thoracic review when every lesion can be removed; a prior lung resection does not exclude liver resection.

Portal (hepatoduodenal) nodes: resect only with complete lymphadenectomy after response to chemotherapy, with explicit counselling; coeliac, para-aortic and retroperitoneal nodes generally not. Portal and retroperitoneal nodes did equally poorly in the largest single-institution series (MSKCC); a Paris series found pedicular nodes better than coeliac or para-aortic nodes (5-year survival 25% vs 0%).
Peritoneum: limited peritoneal disease with liver metastases only in a peritoneal-surface-malignancy centre (CRS/HIPEC plus limited liver resection).
Counsel: recurrence about 90%; 10-year disease-free survival about 3% after resection with extrahepatic disease.
questions.rationale: Pooled and registry data show useful survival after complete resection of lung disease and poorer survival with nodal or peritoneal disease; the only randomized trial of lung metastasectomy was inconclusive.

studies.population: Meta-analysis, 52 studies, 15,144 patients (2,308 with extrahepatic disease). Synchronous or previous extrahepatic disease resected with the liver.
studies.results: 5-year survival: lung 26% (15–39%), peritoneum 17%, nodes 15%; R0 at both sites lowered the risk of death (RR 0.73).
studies.limits: Nodal locations pooled; selected series.
studies.locator: HPB 2016; Results.

studies.population: MSKCC, 219 hepatectomies with resected extrahepatic disease. Synchronous disease, resected within 6 months.
studies.results: Portal vs retroperitoneal nodes: no survival difference (p=0.768); incomplete extrahepatic resection: no survivors beyond 3.5 years; disease-free at 10 years 3.2%.
studies.limits: Selected; tables not available.
studies.locator: Ann Surg 2017; Results.

studies.population: Randomized trial, 93 patients. Lung metastases after colorectal resection.
studies.results: Adjusted HR 0.87 (0.51–1.48); inconclusive.
studies.limits: Underpowered.
studies.locator: Colorectal Dis 2020.

studies.population: Cancer Care Ontario guideline (archived December 2020; evidence to January 2010). Liver and lung metastases.
studies.results: Combined or staged metastasectomy recommended when all lung metastases can be removed; liver resection may follow a prior lung resection; routine liver resection not recommended with portal nodal disease.
studies.limits: Archived; non-comparative series.
studies.locator: Curr Oncol 2013; Recommendation 1.

studies.population: LiverMetSurvey registry. 149 liver plus lung resections vs 9,185 liver-only.
studies.results: Adjusted 5-year survival 44.5% vs 51.5%; 14.3% when lung disease was not resected.
studies.limits: Registry; selected minority.
studies.locator: Br J Surg 2015 (abstract; full text pending).

studies.population: Single centre, 47 hepatectomies with lymphadenectomy. Nodes after chemotherapy.
studies.results: 5-year survival 25% pedicular vs 0% coeliac or para-aortic.
studies.limits: Small, older series.
studies.locator: J Clin Oncol 2008 (abstract; full text pending).

studies.population: Meta-analysis, 17 studies, 988 patients. Synchronous peritoneal and liver metastases.
studies.results: CRS/HIPEC with liver treatment: 5-year survival 37%.
studies.limits: Retrospective, selected.
studies.locator: Ann Surg Oncol 2025 (abstract; full text pending).

studies.population: Meta-analysis, 9 studies, 746 patients. Peritoneal disease with vs without liver metastases.
studies.results: Overall survival HR 1.68 with liver metastases.
studies.limits: Observational.
studies.locator: Int J Hyperthermia 2020 (abstract; full text pending).

questions.counter: Benefit is not proven by randomization; lung metastasectomy itself was inconclusive in PulMiCC.
questions.change: Randomized data on metastasectomy in combined liver and lung disease.

positions.says: Ten of 91 evaluated patients transplanted at three centres, 1.5-year survival 100% and recurrence-free survival 62%. Roadmap critique: tiny, single-arm and short, non-transplanted patients unreported; the commentary calls it a technical demonstration.

positions.says: With a standardised remnant under 30%, ALPPS achieved resection in 92% versus 57% with two-stage hepatectomy. Roadmap critique: endpoint was resectability not survival, grade 3a+ complications 43% in both arms, 90-day mortality 8.3% versus 6.1%, volumetry left to local practice.

positions.says: Rescue ALPPS after failed portal occlusion narrowed the gap (82% versus 92%, not significant), so embolisation-first with ALPPS in reserve is not excluded; two-stage completion of 57% fell below published 60–75% under the strict 30% threshold.
positions.locator: Gate 3 · Reasonable options 'Portal vein embolisation or liver venous deprivation' and 'Two-stage hepatectomy'

positions.says: Mandates resectability assessment at baseline and every two to three months but defines neither resectability nor an adequate future liver remnant.

positions.says: Declares resectability, future liver remnant and staged hepatectomy out of scope, so it offers no threshold or augmentation guidance.
positions.locator: Appendix: what is wrong with each paper · ASCO 2023

questions.divergence: Only LIGRO compares augmentation routes, on resectability rather than survival, and neither ESMO nor ASCO defines an adequate remnant, so the thresholds and the hierarchy are local policy.
questions.proposal: Least invasive first: portal vein embolisation or liver venous deprivation, then staged hepatectomy, with ALPPS in reserve for a fit patient whose remnant will not reach threshold in time, at a centre doing it regularly. The order reflects morbidity and the LIGRO rescue finding, not survival; thresholds, hierarchy, decider and embolisation-to-surgery interval need hepatobiliary and IR approval (grade D).

questions.audit: Perioperative safety measure by procedure type, including augmentation and staged strategies, plus resection rate and dropout between stages.

questions.title: No tumor is visible after treatment
questions.question: How do we handle PET-negative/disappearing lesions or radiographic NED?
questions.status: No transplant for presumed microscopic disease · not activated
questions.context: No visible tumor after treatment is a reason to reassess the indication; presumed microscopic disease alone does not justify transplantation.

positions.says: “4 (57.1%) of the 7 patients who demonstrated complete radiographic response harbored viable carcinoma on explant pathology.” Imaging can miss viable tumor; this selected series does not prove comparative benefit from transplanting all NED patients.
positions.locator: Published PDF p1 / journal pe1026, abstract Results

questions.proposal: Do not activate LT solely for presumed microscopic disease in radiographic NED; separate residual cancer from treatment-related liver failure.
rules: Residual unresectable disease: convincing viable/suspicious disease on appropriate cross-sectional imaging may proceed to B1 review even if PET is negative. PET negativity alone does not prove cure.

Radiographic NED/occult-residual-risk: no convincing remaining disease on high-quality staging. Maintain the original lesion map, continue appropriate oncology care and reassess in about eight weeks; LT for presumed microscopic risk requires a separately approved NED study.

Irreversible treatment-related liver failure: evaluate a separate liver-failure indication with independent hepatology and oncologic-suitability review. Do not relabel it active unresectable cancer. Do not stop effective treatment to provoke recurrence or biopsy every scar.

Keep all original lesion sites mapped. Disappearance does not establish eradication, but uncertain microscopic viability alone does not establish persistent unresectability or transplant benefit; diagnostic accuracy and treatment benefit are different questions.
questions.tests: Expert comparison of pretreatment and current liver MRI/CT; systemic staging; treatment dates and PET interpretation; liver reserve; separate adjudication of NED versus suspicious residual sites.
questions.allocation: A separate liver-failure indication does not automatically meet the CRLM exception pathway. Obtain case-specific clinical and allocation adjudication.
questions.rationale: CT/MRI/PET negativity cannot reliably establish pathological eradication. However, uncertain residual microscopic disease also does not automatically establish clinically meaningful persistent unresectability or an LT benefit. DREAM provides the crucial balance: substantial residual risk despite disappearance, but no adequately powered proof that removing every invisible site improves survival. The small US LT series is genuine NED/injury experience but remains selected and uncontrolled.
questions.counter: Some disappearing lesions are genuinely nonviable: DREAM classified 95/152 CT-plus-MRI disappearing lesions as nonviable by pathology or two-year observation; Oba found only 3/68 viable lesions after negative MRI plus CE-IOUS. Conversely, 4/7 complete imaging responders in the explant series had viable cancer. Both prevent a binary 'all scars count' or 'none count' rule. NED patients with preserved liver function lack comparative evidence of benefit from prophylactic LT.
questions.certainty: Moderate certainty that imaging disappearance does not reliably prove nonviability; low certainty about the best lesion-management strategy; very low certainty for LT in true radiographic NED or treatment-injury subgroups. Explant findings are diagnostic, not a causal efficacy comparison.
questions.threshold_basis: No validated chemotherapy-cycle minimum, scar count, PET-negative interval, ctDNA-negativity requirement or NED duration establishes LT benefit. Proposed approximately eight-week imaging while on active treatment is local workflow, adjustable for clinical need; more sensitive imaging/CE-IOUS informs resection planning but is not a transplant clearance test.

studies.population: Retrospective radiology–explant study of 14 selected LT recipients; eight indications were unresectable disease and six treatment-associated liver failure/biliary complications. Median 11 original lesions and 24 chemotherapy cycles; extensive systemic/local therapy. Seven had PET-defined complete radiographic response. This was a transplanted-only, highly selected sample.
studies.results: Explant contained viable carcinoma in 11/14; nine had additional lesions not accounted for on pre-LT imaging. Four of seven imaging complete responders still had viable tumour. The three pathological complete responders were all in the liver-failure indication group.
studies.limits: Demonstrates imperfect imaging negative predictive value, not that every scar remains viable or that prophylactic LT improves survival for radiographic NED. studies.locator: Ann Surg 2023;278:e1026–e1034; full PDF methods, radiology/explant correlation tables, Results and Discussion.

Primary diagnostic analysis had 152 evaluable CT-plus-MRI disappearing lesions from 44 patients. Post-treatment CT plus MRI (diffusion, T1/T2 and contrast); disappearance on both defined confirmed DLM. Reference was pathology for resected sites or no site recurrence over two years for unresected sites. Fifty-one confirmed lesions were non-evaluable, including deaths and incomplete imaging follow-up.
studies.results: Nonviability NPV was 62.5% (95/152; 90% CI 50.8–74.2), failing the prespecified >85% benchmark; CT-alone NPV 52.9%. Resected confirmed DLM: 50/88 nonviable; left-behind: 45/64 without site recurrence. In the n=45 R0/1, no-extrahepatic-disease subgroup, resecting all confirmed DLM (19 patients) versus leaving at least one (26) yielded DFS HR 0.92 (95% CI 0.48–1.77), OS HR 0.80 (0.21–3.08), with time measured after surgery; survival comparisons were not powered or randomized. Median follow-up 26.1 months.
studies.limits: Lesion-level diagnostic probability is not patient-level benefit. Two-year non-recurrence is not pathology; evaluability selection and noncentral imaging review are limitations. Neither disappearance equals cure nor uncertain viability requires removal/LT. A nonsignificant survival comparison is not equivalence or evidence that resection is futile.
studies.locator: JAMA Surg 2025 DOI10.1001/jamasurg.2025.3600; PDF E1–E3 design/endpoint; E5 Figure 1 and survival; E7 Figure 4/limitations.

studies.population: Retrospective hepatectomy imaging series, 184 patients, 59 with 275 CT-disappearing metastases; primary published abstract verified, full PDF pending. studies.limits: Lesion-level retrospective selection and assay sequence differ from DREAM. More sensitive imaging can identify residual disease, but these data do not prove that every original site must be resected or that NED warrants LT.

studies.results: Median follow-up 700 days; three recurrences. Reported RFS one year 6/8 (75%) and two years 3/5 (60%) reflects very small mature denominators.
studies.limits: This is actual published experience with NED/injury routes, so it must not be described as nonexistent; it is not controlled proof of benefit or a universal cycle-count requirement. studies.locator: Liver Transpl 2024;30:1238–1249; PMID38833301 published abstract; complete methods pending.

studies.population: Multicentre open-label randomized trial, 20 European centres, 157 screened and 94 randomized (47 LT-plus-chemotherapy, 47 chemotherapy); 63 screened excluded, including 13 with equivocal unresectability and 36 with progression. questions.title: Molecular findings and other initial limits
questions.question: Which molecular or extrahepatic expansions should be studied?
questions.status: Initial selection and expansion limits · not activated
questions.context: Review molecular markers, CEA, primary-tumor margins and treatment timing. Previous extrahepatic disease has its own review (CRLM-B5).

positions.says: “BRAF wild type, microsatellite stable” Molecular guidance is more specific than simply “favorable biology”; KRAS is not stated as a blanket exclusion.

positions.says: “Median disease-free and overall survival was 4 and 18 months respectively.” Poor outcomes after multiple simultaneous relaxations caution against broad expansion; the study does not isolate any one criterion’s causal effect.
positions.locator: Published PDF p1 / journal p467, abstract Results

questions.proposal: Do not open molecular expansions initially; permit KRAS-mutant disease when all other selected criteria are met. Previous extrahepatic disease follows CRLM-B5.
rules: Initial proposed exclusions: BRAF-mutant disease, MSI-H/dMMR disease, R1 primary margins, pretreatment liver lesion >10 cm, or progression despite treatment. Previous extrahepatic disease is addressed separately in CRLM-B5. Preserve these as separate research questions; do not combine several relaxations.
Proposed CEA requirement: strictly <80 ng/mL, including initial activation. Repeat a borderline/unexpected result and review the trajectory; a falling value still ≥80 does not clear this local rule.

Require ≥6 months of documented control and the applicable ≥12-month CRLM-diagnosis interval. Report ordinary RECIST separately from the NLRB >10% wording; new lesions or concerning growth are HOLD pending central measurement review.

Confirmed progression resets the proposed six-month control clock after subsequent effective treatment; one improved scan is insufficient. Use the actual application imaging/CEA windows. Do not delay indicated primary surgery to manufacture eligibility.
questions.tests: Primary R0 pathology; BRAF, RAS and MMR/MSI; original maximum lesion diameter; complete EHD history; dated CEA; dated response and primary/CRLM diagnosis; current staging.

questions.title: Expected benefit, recurrence and graft use
questions.question: How much recurrence/graft use is acceptable for the observed survival benefit?
questions.context: Compare expected benefit with continued nontransplant treatment and discuss recurrence and future graft use.

where.label: Request and renew the MELD exception

positions.says: “three (8%) of 36 patients who received a transplant were retransplanted” Additional graft use is real. The 36 per-protocol recipients differ from the 40-recipient safety population.
positions.locator: Published PDF p9 / journal p1115, Results

questions.proposal: Accept that recurrence may coexist with meaningful survival benefit, but plan one graft and account for recurrence treatment and all additional graft use.
rules: Before considering transplantation: a patient-specific benefit comparison against accessible non-LT care, feasible recurrence-treatment options, and a realistic local wait/treatment plan. Reassess about every eight weeks while waiting; no unsupported maximum-wait exclusion is imposed.

Plan one graft per recipient; no planned retransplantation for oncologic recurrence. Rescue of early nononcologic graft failure remains a separate standard transplant/allocation decision and is never promised or withheld by this rule.

No low recurrence-rate/RFS cutoff is substituted for survival or quality-of-life benefit. Record all-screened outcomes, recurrence treatment burden, time off therapy, graft loss/retransplantation and functional recovery. Apply the one-event early safety pause in ALLOC-B4 to newly activated experimental cohorts.
questions.tests: Contemporary comparator; current fitness/control; recurrence options; local access estimate; patient priorities; graft-use and follow-up plan.
questions.allocation: Do not promise trial survival where waiting/access differ materially. Count all grafts and downstream allocation consequences, including LDLT recipients who later need DDLT.
questions.rationale: The relevant endpoint is the entire strategy from a shared eligibility/randomization date: access to a first graft, wait-list progression, perioperative death, graft failure, recurrence, salvage treatment, long-term survival and QoL. Recurrence does not erase all benefit, but is a substantial burden; SECA-II shows both long post-recurrence survival and late metastatic death. TransMet's 56.6% ITT survival is the appropriate randomized headline, with 73.3% PP provided only secondarily.
questions.counter: TransMet's nine progression dropouts and three retransplants show why post-LT survival alone is inadequate. The 2026 SECA-II ten-year OS was 51.5%, not its five-year 77.8%; four metastatic deaths occurred after five years. Arm D's 18-month median OS cautions against assuming every expanded candidate obtains sufficient benefit. Selected HAIP/conversion patients can have durable survival without a graft, but cross-study comparisons cannot calculate an individual's LT gain.
questions.certainty: Moderate-to-high for a survival advantage in selected TransMet patients; low for an individual numerical benefit model, long-wait extrapolation, high-risk graft strategies or predetermined retransplant policy. Long-term SECA-II is informative but small and uncontrolled.
questions.threshold_basis: No validated minimum RFS, individual five-year benefit percentage or fixed number of salvage operations establishes acceptable LT value. The two-year/three-year thresholds sometimes used in economic models are not recipient-selection validation. One planned graft and safety-review triggers are institutional ethical/operational proposals.

studies.population: Multicentre open-label randomized trial, 20 European centres, 157 screened and 94 randomized (47 LT-plus-chemotherapy, 47 chemotherapy); 63 screened excluded, including 13 with equivocal unresectability and 36 with progression. Age 18–65; ECOG 0–1; R0 colorectal primary; BRAF nonmutated; no prior or current extrahepatic disease/local recurrence; chemotherapy response or stable disease for at least 3 months, at most three lines. CEA <80 ng/mL OR at least 50% reduction from peak was permitted. Independent committee of at least two surgeons, two oncologists and one radiologist reviewed original and current lesion maps. These are trial criteria, not identical to current NLRB guidance.
studies.results: Primary time origin was randomization. Median follow-up 59.3 months. Five-year ITT OS was 56.6% versus 12.6% (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.21–0.65); per-protocol OS 73.3% versus 9.3%. Of 47 assigned LT, 38 received LT and 36 were per-protocol; nine had progression-related exclusion/dropout. The control arm included seven subsequent resections and two LT crossovers. Safety population comprised 40 grafted patients. Among 36 per-protocol LT recipients, 26 recurred; 19/26 received chemotherapy and 12/26 local curative-intent treatment. Median per-protocol PFS was 17.4 versus 6.4 months, and secondary PFS after salvage was 35.4 months in the LT arm. Three of 36 per-protocol recipients required retransplantation (primary nonfunction, donor gallbladder cancer, caval obstruction/large-for-size); one postoperative death was reported. Serious adverse events occurred in 32/40 safety LT recipients. Median wait to LT was 50.5 days, which limits transfer to longer-wait systems.
studies.limits: Strong evidence for the selected trial population, not for BRAF-mutant, ECOG 2, active extrahepatic, truly NED, resectable or broadly expanded disease. PP survival conditions on reaching treatment and must not replace ITT. The Results recurrence denominator is 26/36; Figure 3 caption says 28 recurrences, consistent with a broader all-grafted report, so do not mix these denominators. QoL collection had only 55/74 per-protocol baseline questionnaires and is descriptive, not proof of a large QoL gain. Priority allocation and rapid access were part of the treatment strategy.
studies.locator: Lancet 2024;404:1107–1118. PDF pp.2–4 eligibility/committee; pp.5–6 trial flow/Table 1; pp.8–9 recurrence, safety, retransplantation, Figure 3; p.10 QoL/limitations.

studies.population: Prospective SECA-II extended follow-up, 25 recipients from April 2012 to November 2023; analysis cutoff 1 January 2025. Includes the original SECA-II cohort. All grafted under SECA-II included. At least one year diagnosis to inclusion and no progression required; one inadvertently transplanted patient had progression on a scan not available to the transplant centre. One early postoperative death was included in survival analyses but excluded from other analyses, so baseline Table 1 denominator is 24. Among these 24, median largest lesion 24 mm (4–48), CEA 3.5 (1–33), PET MTV 7.3 cm³ (0–139); only two MTV >70, two KRAS-mutated, one right-sided ascending primary and one pN2. Oslo scores 0/1/2 were 9/13/2.
studies.results: Time zero LT; median follow-up of survivors 97.2 months. Median OS 128.2 months (95% CI 74.8–181.6); five- and ten-year OS 77.8% and 51.5%. Median RFS 24.3 months; 12/25 relapsed, six initially lung-only. Median post-recurrence survival 62.9 months (25.7–101.1); nine had surgery as first recurrence treatment, but only three were classified curative-intent at that first treatment. Twelve had no recurrence over median 74 months; four exceeded ten years without recurrence. Four patients died of metastases more than five years after LT. Reported serious complications: five grade IIIa, three IIIb, one grade V hepatic-artery-thrombosis death.
studies.limits: No contemporaneous control and only 25 recipients; highly favorable biology cannot justify broad expansion. Abstract speculates up to 15 potentially cured, body p.5 says up to 13; neither is an observed, validated cure fraction. Use observed survival/recurrence instead. The discussion's assertion that RFS is not valid for efficacy should not erase recurrence burden, treatment harms or QoL; RFS is insufficient alone, not unimportant. Updated survival supersedes rather than adds an independent 83% SECA-II estimate.
studies.locator: Ann Surg 2026 early report DOI 10.1097/SLA.0000000000007200; PDF p.2 methods/time origins and early-death handling; p.3 Table 1 and outcomes; pp.4–5 salvage, late death, cure-count discrepancy and complications.

studies.population: Prospective SECA-II arm D expanded-criteria cohort, ten recipients, without control. Expanded both recipient and donor criteria, including resectable pulmonary metastases and omission of previous stringent response/time restrictions. Eight had pN2 primaries, six poorly differentiated or signet-ring pathology, five right-sided cancers; median 20 liver lesions and largest diameter 59 mm. This was a bundle of adverse features, not an isolated prior-lung-metastasis experiment.
studies.results: From LT, median DFS four months and median OS 18 months. Rapid recurrence and limited survival contrast with strictly selected SECA-II, despite use of donor grafts intended to broaden access.
studies.limits: Very small and uncontrolled; simultaneous biologic, anatomic and donor expansions prevent estimating the independent effect of prior pulmonary disease, BRAF status, grade or donor quality. Negative experience argues against opening several expansions at once, not that every single deviation has proven futility.
studies.locator: BJS Open 2020;4:467–477; full text methods, Tables 1–3 and survival figures.

studies.population: Single-centre retrospective HAIP cohort: 1,110 patients treated in 2006–2016, 483 initially unresectable after exclusions; 83 met modified transplant criteria, but only 23 were pretreated, chemotherapy-controlled transplant-like candidates. Selected patients had liver-confined disease without progression on pre-HAIP chemotherapy. The study modified SECA/TransMet criteria: PET, molecular profile, CEA and standardized RECIST response were not mandatory, and primary resection could occur during/after HAIP. Applying at least one year from CRC diagnosis to HAIP left only five of 483 patients. Unresectability considered adequate functional remnant, vascular/biliary preservation and intraoperative ultrasound, not lesion number alone.
studies.results: Time zero was HAIP placement, not a common LT-versus-HAIP eligibility date. In the 23 selected pretreated patients, 18/23 (78%) converted to resection; only 10/18 were R0, and 17/18 recurred, with salvage treatment in 15. Median follow-up was 97.7 months; median OS 61 months (95% CI 36–92), five-year OS 53% (36–79), PFS 13 months (9.6–22), hepatic PFS 16 months (11–61). Median treatment comprised five HAIP cycles and nine systemic cycles. Biliary sclerosis requiring stents occurred in 3/23 (13%); one pump-arterial dissection required revision.
studies.limits: Selection from a large denominator, modified eligibility, expert-centre availability, retrospective ascertainment and a different time origin prohibit equivalence claims against TransMet. The high conversion rate is clinically important counterevidence to declaring unresectability before specialist conversion review. It does not make HAIP compulsory or establish that its toxicities are an indication to create for LT.
studies.locator: Complete accepted manuscript, PDF pp.6–11: cohort derivation, modified criteria, conversion, survival and adverse events; subsequent tables.

studies.population: Single-centre intensive pre-LT locoregional-treatment protocol: 27 evaluated, 16 included, nine transplanted (seven living donor). Abstract-only verification. Median 16 systemic cycles (10–40); Y90 in five, ablation in four, resection in four and HAIP in three. Five grafted patients had no detectable disease and four had treatment-induced cirrhosis.
studies.results: Median follow-up 700 days; three recurrences. Reported RFS one year 6/8 (75%) and two years 3/5 (60%) reflects very small mature denominators.
studies.limits: This is actual published experience with NED/injury routes, so it must not be described as nonexistent; it is not controlled proof of benefit or a universal cycle-count requirement. Patients likely overlap occult-explant/PET/ctDNA cohorts. Do not intensify treatment to manufacture liver failure.
studies.locator: Liver Transpl 2024;30:1238–1249; PMID38833301 published abstract; complete methods pending.

studies.population: Official Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology guidance, December 2025 posting checked 24 October 2026. Allocation-review guidance, not national clinical policy or proof of efficacy. CRLM: BRAF wild type, microsatellite stable, R0 primary, at least 12 months from CRLM diagnosis and six months chemotherapy control; pretreatment largest lesion not >10 cm; no post-primary-resection extrahepatic disease, including nodes outside the primary field. Initial CEA exclusion is >80 ng/mL; extensions require <80. NET: known portal-drained GEP primary, well-differentiated G1/G2, Ki-67 <20%, primary and extrahepatic disease resected with at least six months NED; no active extrahepatic disease. Lung/bone/other solid-organ metastasis history is a permanent exception-guidance exclusion.
studies.results: No efficacy denominator. NET guidance has no explicit numerical age or hepatic-volume cutoff. CRLM wording excludes >10% diameter growth or new lesions and labels this RECIST 1.1, although conventional RECIST 1.1 progression generally uses at least 20% summed-diameter increase plus an absolute change; record both, do not silently equate them.
studies.limits: Clinical judgment, exception endorsement and graft availability are distinct. A reasonable research hypothesis or living donor does not override allocation guidance or demonstrate acceptable benefit. At exactly CEA 80 the initial/extension wording differs; the draft's strict <80 harmonization is a conservative local rule.
studies.locator: Official PDF NET pp.8–9; CRLM pp.9–10; introduction on purpose/status.

questions.title: Previously treated extrahepatic disease
questions.question: Should a lung-only study stratum be opened for completely treated pulmonary metastases, and if so with which interval and biology limits? All other previously treated extrahepatic sites stay closed.
questions.status: Closed · lung-only study proposed · not activated
questions.context: Use when colorectal cancer has involved any site outside the liver (after primary resection, removed together with the primary, or as local relapse), including disease later resected, ablated, irradiated or in response to treatment.
questions.proposal: Keep previously treated extrahepatic disease closed in the initial CRLM pathway. Propose one narrow study stratum for limited, completely treated lung-only metastases; every other site stays closed.
rules: Default: extrahepatic metastasis after primary resection (including nodes outside the primary resection field), extrahepatic metastasis removed with the primary, and local relapse are outside the initial pathway, even after resection, ablation, radiotherapy or complete response. Response to systemic therapy alone never counts as clearance.

Proposed lung-only study stratum (not active; needs its own protocol, institutional and IRB approval, and a living-donor or individually reviewed allocation route): pulmonary metastases only, at most three lesions in total, each completely treated with curative intent (R0 resection preferred; stereotactic radiotherapy or ablation only with documented local control), no thoracic nodal involvement on pathology or PET-CT, and no recurrence outside the liver for ≥12 months after the last lung treatment.

The stratum adds no other relaxation: every CRLM-B3 limit still applies (BRAF wild type, MSS/pMMR, R0 primary, CEA <80 ng/mL, no pretreatment liver lesion >10 cm, documented disease control), and chest CT and PET-CT within one month show no disease outside the liver. Do not combine it with another expansion.

Hilar nodes: frozen section of hilar nodes before implantation, and before donor hepatectomy in living donation; a positive node ends the transplant. In Oslo, 7 of 72 listed patients were stopped at laparotomy for hilar nodal metastasis.

Closed, with no proposed stratum: nodal disease outside the primary resection field; peritoneal, ovarian, adrenal, bone, brain or other non-lung sites; local relapse; more than three lung lesions; thoracic nodal involvement; or recurrence after lung treatment. A new or indeterminate extrahepatic lesion during evaluation or on the waiting list is HOLD for characterization and restaging; it does not enter the stratum.
questions.tests: Dated history of every extrahepatic site: imaging, operative and pathology reports, radiotherapy or ablation records and margins; thoracic nodal status; number and size of lung lesions; interval from primary resection to lung disease and from the last lung treatment to evaluation; chest CT and PET-CT within one month; dated CEA series. Plan intraoperative hilar node frozen section before implantation (and before donor hepatectomy).
questions.allocation: NLRB guidance excludes extrahepatic disease after primary tumor resection (including lymphadenopathy outside the primary lymph-node resection) and local relapse from an initial CRLM MELD exception, and requires no development of extrahepatic disease for extension. A standardized deceased-donor exception is therefore not available. The lung-only stratum would need living-donor transplantation within an approved study or an individual NLRB request that states the deviation; this proposal implies neither.
questions.rationale: Lung-limited colorectal metastasis is the most indolent extrahepatic pattern, and the transplant experience points the same way. On retrospective review of SECA-I chest CT, 7 of 21 recipients already had untreated pulmonary metastases at transplantation, and 6 of them were among the longest survivors; no statistical test was reported. Lung metastases after transplantation grew no faster than in non-transplanted controls (median doubling time 125 versus 130 days), and the 14 Oslo recipients whose lung recurrence was resected had 64.5% ten-year survival from lung resection. IHPBA advises that isolated pulmonary recurrence after transplantation be considered for resection. Newer protocols admit limited, treated lung disease: SECA-III excludes recent resection of non-hepatic metastases and any previous bone, CNS or thoracic or abdominal nodal metastasis, and a Japanese living-donor study accepts up to three treated lung metastases without recurrence for more than six months. This supports studying a lung-only stratum, not opening it.
questions.counter: Direct evidence is one patient. In SECA-II arm D, the recipient whose lung metastasis had been resected eight years earlier was recurrence-free at 23 months, but the arm overall did poorly (median DFS 4 months, OS 18 months) because several adverse features were combined. IHPBA states there is no evidence to support transplantation in patients who present with or subsequently develop extrahepatic metastases; TransMet excluded prior or current extrahepatic disease and local recurrence; and NLRB excludes post-resection extrahepatic disease. In PulMiCC, lung metastasectomy did not clearly improve survival (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.56–1.56), so successful lung treatment may select favourable biology rather than cure it. After liver resection, nodal and peritoneal extrahepatic disease had markedly shorter survival than lung disease (median 26 and 29 versus 45 months).
questions.certainty: Very low for transplantation after previously treated extrahepatic disease (one reported recipient); low for the indirect inference that lung-limited disease behaves indolently after transplantation; no transplant evidence for previous nodal, peritoneal or other sites.
questions.threshold_basis: At most three lung lesions follows the Japanese living-donor protocol. Twelve months without recurrence after lung treatment sits between that protocol (more than six months) and SECA-III, which excludes resection of non-hepatic metastases within the last two years and of pulmonary or liver-hilum lymph-node metastases within the last year. Excluding thoracic nodal involvement reflects its strong adverse effect after lung metastasectomy in patients with previously resected liver metastases (HR 4.86). None of these limits has been tested in transplant recipients.

studies.population: Multicentre randomized trial of liver transplantation plus chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone; 94 randomized. Required no extrahepatic disease and excluded prior or current extrahepatic disease and local recurrence.
studies.results: Five-year overall survival 56.6% versus 12.6% by intention to treat (HR 0.37).
studies.limits: Provides no data on patients with previous extrahepatic disease; its benefit cannot be extrapolated to them.
studies.locator: Lancet 2024; eligibility criteria in Methods.

studies.population: 2021 international Delphi consensus on transplantation for non-resectable colorectal liver metastases. Statement 9: there is no evidence to support transplantation in patients who initially present with or subsequently develop extrahepatic or extracolonic metastases. Statements 10–12: high-resolution chest CT and FDG PET-CT to rule out extrahepatic disease; nodal sampling when suspicion is high and PET is inconclusive.
studies.results: Statement 41: isolated pulmonary recurrence after transplantation should be considered for resection. The text notes that many lung recurrences were retrospectively visible at transplantation and do not grow faster under immunosuppression.
studies.limits: Expert consensus. It treats extrahepatic disease as a sign of disseminated disease and does not separately address completely treated lung-only disease.
studies.locator: Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2021;6:933–946; statements 9–12 and 41, recurrence discussion.

studies.population: Prospective SECA-II arm D expanded-criteria cohort; ten recipients. Unlike SECA-I and SECA-II, patients with resectable pulmonary metastases or previous resection of pulmonary metastases were eligible. One recipient had a pulmonary metastasis resected eight years before transplantation (node-negative sigmoid primary, at most two liver metastases).
studies.results: Only two of ten were recurrence-free (23 and 26 months); one was the recipient with the previously resected lung metastasis. A second recipient had an ovarian metastasis removed with the primary 14 months before transplantation and relapsed in the lung at 5 months. Overall median DFS 4 months and OS 18 months; the lung was the first relapse site in six.
studies.limits: One relevant patient within a cohort that combined several adverse biological, anatomical and donor features; it cannot estimate the effect of prior lung disease.
studies.locator: BJS Open 2020;4:467–477; Methods, Table 2 (patient 1) and Discussion.

studies.population: Prospective SECA-I cohort, 21 recipients; recurrence-pattern analysis with re-review of pre-transplant chest CT. Liver-only disease was required at inclusion.
studies.results: Thirteen of 16 single-site first recurrences were pulmonary; on retrospective review, 7 recipients already had untreated pulmonary metastases at transplantation and 6 were among the longest survivors.
studies.limits: Small cohort; the lesions were untreated and found retrospectively; no statistical test; not evidence that treated lung disease is safe.
studies.locator: Ann Surg Oncol 2014; Results (full text).

studies.population: Case–control imaging study: 11 SECA recipients with 18 resected lung metastases versus 12 non-transplanted rectal cancer controls. Lung metastases arising after transplantation.
studies.results: Median tumour-volume doubling time 125 versus 130 days by diameter; five-year overall survival after first pulmonary resection 51% in the transplant group.
studies.limits: Small selected groups; addresses growth after transplantation, not eligibility after previous lung disease.
studies.locator: Br J Surg; abstract.

studies.population: Oslo cohort: 14 of 55 recipients whose first relapse was pulmonary and treated by resection. Pre-transplant liver PET metabolic tumour volume (MTV) used for stratification.
studies.results: Ten-year overall survival from lung resection 64.5%; 85.7% with MTV <70 cm³ versus 25.0% above. Eight had no evidence of disease 7–131 months after lung resection.
studies.limits: Post-transplant recurrence in a small selected group; does not test transplantation after treated lung disease.
studies.locator: Cancers 2022;14:5042; Results.

studies.population: Oslo randomized trial of transplantation versus chemotherapy or other treatment after progression on, or intolerance of, first-line chemotherapy; target 30. Allows resectable lung lesions, all <15 mm. Excludes previous resection of local relapse or non-hepatic metastasis within the last 2 years or resection of pulmonary or liver hilus lymph node metastases in the last year, and previously diagnosed bone, CNS or thoracic/abdominal nodal metastases.
studies.results: Recruiting; no results posted.
studies.limits: Registry wording for a different population (progression on first-line therapy); eligibility may change.
studies.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03494946, eligibility criteria (current version).

studies.population: Japanese multicentre single-arm living-donor transplantation protocol (11 university hospitals; target 23). No distant metastasis except the liver, but patients with no more than three lung metastases and no recurrence for more than six months after treatment are eligible; RAS and BRAF mutations are not exclusions; central eligibility review. No size limit is set.
studies.results: Protocol only; outcomes not yet reported.
studies.limits: The authors describe the criteria as relatively broad; no control arm.
studies.locator: BMJ Open 2024; eligibility criteria and strengths/limitations.

studies.population: Randomized trial of pulmonary metastasectomy versus no metastasectomy; 93 randomized at 14 hospitals. One to six resectable lung metastases at a median 2.7 years after colorectal resection; 29% had prior liver metastasectomy.
studies.results: Adjusted hazard ratio for death within five years 0.87 (0.51–1.48; unadjusted 0.93, 0.56–1.56); five-year survival 36.4% with metastasectomy versus 29.6% without.
studies.limits: Closed at 31% of the planned 300; inconclusive; not a transplant population.
studies.locator: Colorectal Dis 2020; Results (full text).

studies.source: Salah 2014 · lung metastasectomy after liver resection
studies.population: Pooled individual-patient analysis of 146 patients undergoing pulmonary metastasectomy after previous curative liver resection (five studies). Lung metastases detected a median 23 months after liver resection.
studies.results: Five-year overall survival 54.4% and recurrence-free survival 29.3% from lung resection; thoracic lymph-node involvement was the only independent adverse factor (HR 4.86, 95% CI 1.56–15.14).
studies.limits: Retrospective selected surgical series; not transplant recipients.
studies.locator: Ann Surg Oncol; abstract.

studies.population: Systematic review of liver resection for CRLM with extrahepatic disease: 50 studies, 3481 patients. Hepatic resection in the presence of extrahepatic disease; heterogeneous timing and treatment.
studies.results: Median survival by extrahepatic site: lung 45 months, portal or para-aortic nodes 26 months, peritoneum 29 months.
studies.limits: Non-transplant, heterogeneous observational studies.
studies.locator: Eur J Cancer 2014; abstract.

studies.population: Official OPTN/NLRB guidance: Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology. CRLM exclusions for an initial exception: extrahepatic disease after primary tumor resection (including lymphadenopathy outside the primary lymph-node resection) and local relapse. Extension requires no development of extrahepatic disease. Staging: CT/MRI of chest, abdomen and pelvis and PET within one month of the initial request.
studies.results: Allocation guidance; no outcome data.
studies.limits: Governs MELD-exception review, not clinical suitability or living-donor eligibility.
studies.locator: Official PDF, CRLM section.

studies.population: Oslo pooled cohort; 72 listed, 61 transplanted. PET-CT before transplantation; prior extrahepatic disease not analysed.
studies.results: 10 of 72 listed were not transplanted because of extrahepatic disease, 7 with hilar nodal metastasis on frozen section at laparotomy; intention-to-treat 5-year survival 42.6%.
studies.limits: No control group.
studies.locator: JAMA Surg 2023; Results (full text).

studies.population: North American living-donor series; 91 evaluated, 10 transplanted. Liver-confined disease with sustained control; abdominal exploration before the donor operation.
studies.results: 1 of 10 had PET-negative portal nodal metastasis in the explant and recurred in the peritoneum at 121 days.
studies.limits: Ten patients.
studies.locator: JAMA Surg 2022; Table 4 and Results (full text).

shared.title: Separate clinical, allocation, donor and study approval
shared.question: What are we approving?

positions.says: “This resource is not OPTN Policy” Guidance informs case review and is not itself binding policy or a clinical standard.
positions.locator: December 2025 oncology guidance p2, disclaimer

positions.says: “Function independently from the transplant candidate’s team.” Donor advocacy is independent of recipient-team enthusiasm.
positions.locator: Policy 14.2.A, PDF p285, living donor advocate requirements

shared.proposal: Require 100% completion of the applicable clinical, allocation, donor and research determinations before activation.
rules: Complete six separate dated determinations: clinical suitability; standardized-exception eligibility; nonstandard NLRB review status; calculated-MELD access; LDLT donor clearance; and research authorization. Mark nonapplicable domains explicitly with a reason—do not manufacture six approvals for every patient.
Any required missing, pending or adverse determination is a HOLD. An exception application is not approval, a donor is not recipient benefit, and clinical approval is not study activation.
Recheck the current policy/guidance version before each request; record actual decision and priority rather than predicted entitlement.
shared.tests: Signed suitability record; exact allocation route and policy version; exception outcome; donor-team status; study and institutional activation record.
shared.allocation: Policy 9.4 permits discretionary requests where appropriate; absence of favorable diagnosis-specific guidance is not absence of a review mechanism, and a request does not promise approval.
shared.rationale: The separation is a governance requirement, not an empirical survival cutoff. A clinically appropriate patient can lack exception eligibility, and an approved exception does not prove clinical benefit. LDLT requires an independent donor determination; a registry entry is not permission to perform experimental transplantation.
shared.counter: Not every case needs six separate affirmative approvals: several routes are alternatives or not applicable. An indiscriminate six-approval rule could obstruct appropriate standard care.
shared.certainty: High confidence in the separation of applicable authorities; no trial establishes that six boxes improve survival. Local workflow must map to current institutional obligations.
threshold_basis: Six domains: local checklist architecture, not six mandatory national approvals.
100% applicable completion: governance safeguard, not an outcome-derived percentage.
Hold pending required authorization: operational implementation of separate clinical, donor and research responsibilities.

studies.population: Binding OPTN policy posting effective 1 October 2026, checked 24 October 2026. Clinical candidacy, exception scoring, living-donor protection and reporting have different policy sections.
studies.results: Policy 9 governs liver allocation; Policy 14 requires independent donor advocacy/consent; Policy 18 specifies reporting. None establishes a universal cancer-benefit cutoff.
studies.limits: A center’s additional safeguards are not national policy. Review the active text and applicability before individual decisions.
studies.locator: Policies 9, 14.2–14.4 and 18; current official PDF.

studies.population: Current NLRB hepatic-adenoma guidance. Four alternative routes; route four contains conjunctive clinical requirements.
studies.results: GSD/Abernethy; OR unresectable β-catenin-mutated HCA; OR unresectable adenomatosis >10 lesions; OR unresectable, nonoperative-unresponsive and progressive/complicated HCA.
studies.limits: These are review routes, not proof of benefit or a mandatory transplant recommendation. Current text does not require all four conditions simultaneously or cirrhosis for all routes.
studies.locator: December 2025 oncology guidance, hepatic adenoma p11.

studies.population: Federal human-subject protection regulation. Applicability determined by institutional research/regulatory review.
studies.results: 46.111 requires risk minimization, reasonable risk–benefit, equitable selection, informed consent and appropriate monitoring. IRB approval is separate from OPTN allocation and clinical acceptance.
studies.limits: No prescribed ten-patient cap, five-patient interim or one-event statistical boundary; those require protocol-specific design and independent approval.
studies.locator: 45 CFR 46.111(a)(1–7), current official eCFR text checked 24 October 2026.

studies.population: OPTN Ethics Committee white paper, not a trial or binding allocation algorithm. Scarce-organ allocation must balance utility, justice and respect for persons.
studies.results: High predicted recipient survival alone is insufficient: opportunity cost, equity and access also matter. Donor autonomy does not remove clinical obligations.
studies.limits: Provides an ethical framework, not numeric weights, a universal survival threshold or permission to depart from allocation rules.
studies.locator: Introduction; utility/justice/respect-for-persons sections.

shared.title: Assess expected recipient benefit and organ use
shared.question: What is the relevant organ opportunity cost?

positions.says: “intention-to-treat population” The randomized pathway-level comparison is more informative than recipient survival alone; its selection and access conditions still matter.
positions.locator: Published TransMet report, primary analysis description

positions.says: “risks to donors remain incompletely characterized” LDLT transfers some risk to a healthy donor; it does not eliminate the need to establish recipient benefit.
positions.locator: 2026 published report, abstract background

shared.proposal: Require two independent recipient-benefit reviews and an explicit organ-use case; do not adopt a universal five-year survival cutoff.
rules: Proposed requirements: two reviewers not both responsible for recruitment must document expected incremental benefit over the actual contemporary alternative, with unresolved disagreement referred to the full committee.

For DDLT, show local expected access/dropout and sensitivity scenarios at 6, 12 and 18 months, total graft use including retransplantation, and plausible alternative recipients. These are planning scenarios, not imposed waiting periods.

For LDLT, separately show healthy-donor risk and potential downstream deceased-donor graft use. Do not call DCD, extended-criteria grafts or machine perfusion “zero opportunity cost.” No priority changes follow from an AI-selected survival threshold.
shared.tests: Same-eligibility/time-zero comparator; expected access; dropout; donor/graft type; uncertainty intervals; graft loss/retransplant estimate; written independent reviews.
shared.allocation: Only the applicable allocation process determines priority. Favorable post-LT prognosis, evidence grade and urgency are not interchangeable measures.
shared.rationale: Use pathway-level benefit from an agreed entry date, not recipient-only survival. Compare with contemporary tumor-specific care and actual local access. LDLT avoids one direct deceased-donor allocation but creates healthy-donor risk and may generate rescue graft use. Graft quality/perfusion changes do not make opportunity cost zero.
shared.counter: An ambitious prognosis threshold can exclude patients with substantial incremental benefit, while an indolent tumor can have excellent post-LT survival and little incremental benefit. Local wait times and unequal access can reverse a study’s apparent advantage.
shared.certainty: Benefit evidence differs by disease: randomized selected CRLM/HCC pathways cannot be generalized to all expanded indications. Ethical principles are authoritative frameworks, not empirically optimized allocation weights.
threshold_basis: Two reviewers: local independence safeguard, not validated optimum.
6/12/18 months: sensitivity scenarios for access/dropout, not mandatory waits.
HCC ≥60% five-year ITT OS: one expert trial-design benchmark; not a cross-cancer allocation policy.
All grafts: count initial and rescue/retransplant grafts; donor morbidity remains a separate outcome.

studies.population: OPTN Ethics Committee white paper, not a trial or binding allocation algorithm. Scarce-organ allocation must balance utility, justice and respect for persons.
studies.results: High predicted recipient survival alone is insufficient: opportunity cost, equity and access also matter. Donor autonomy does not remove clinical obligations.
studies.limits: Provides an ethical framework, not numeric weights, a universal survival threshold or permission to depart from allocation rules.
studies.locator: Introduction; utility/justice/respect-for-persons sections.

studies.population: Binding OPTN policy posting effective 1 October 2026, checked 24 October 2026. Clinical candidacy, exception scoring, living-donor protection and reporting have different policy sections.
studies.results: Policy 9 governs liver allocation; Policy 14 requires independent donor advocacy/consent; Policy 18 specifies reporting. None establishes a universal cancer-benefit cutoff.
studies.limits: A center’s additional safeguards are not national policy. Review the active text and applicability before individual decisions.
studies.locator: Policies 9, 14.2–14.4 and 18; current official PDF.

studies.population: EASL–AASLD–ILCA 2026 trial-design consensus, LT section. Separates standard/UNOS-DS, expanded intermediate HCC and advanced segmental vascular-invasion research populations.
studies.results: Calls for entry-level dropout/feasibility, ITT EFS/OS and graft/immune harms; discusses ≥60% five-year ITT OS benchmark in HCC.
studies.limits: Expert benchmark, not a validated cross-tumor allocation cutoff or a ten-patient stopping rule; mature five-year endpoints cannot be established after one year.

studies.population: Multicenter randomized phase 2b/3 trial: 74 entered downstaging; 29 dropped out before randomization; 45 responders were randomized, 23 to LT and 22 to nontransplant treatment. studies.locator: Complete accepted manuscript and protocol appendix; final published abstract for survival estimates. Avoid mixing accepted-manuscript and final-publication hazard ratios.

studies.population: Multicentre open-label randomized trial, 20 European centres, 157 screened and 94 randomized (47 LT-plus-chemotherapy, 47 chemotherapy); 63 screened excluded, including 13 with equivocal unresectability and 36 with progression. Age 18–65; ECOG 0–1; R0 colorectal primary; BRAF nonmutated; no prior or current extrahepatic disease/local recurrence; chemotherapy response or stable disease for at least 3 months, at most three lines. CEA <80 ng/mL OR at least 50% reduction from peak was permitted. Independent committee of at least two surgeons, two oncologists and one radiologist reviewed original and current lesion maps. These are trial criteria, not identical to current NLRB guidance.
studies.results: Primary time origin was randomization. Median follow-up 59.3 months. Five-year ITT OS was 56.6% versus 12.6% (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.21–0.65); per-protocol OS 73.3% versus 9.3%. Of 47 assigned LT, 38 received LT and 36 were per-protocol; nine had progression-related exclusion/dropout. The control arm included seven subsequent resections and two LT crossovers. Safety population comprised 40 grafted patients. Among 36 per-protocol LT recipients, 26 recurred; 19/26 received chemotherapy and 12/26 local curative-intent treatment. Median per-protocol PFS was 17.4 versus 6.4 months, and secondary PFS after salvage was 35.4 months in the LT arm. Three of 36 per-protocol recipients required retransplantation (primary nonfunction, donor gallbladder cancer, caval obstruction/large-for-size); one postoperative death was reported. Serious adverse events occurred in 32/40 safety LT recipients. Median wait to LT was 50.5 days, which limits transfer to longer-wait systems.
studies.limits: Strong evidence for the selected trial population, not for BRAF-mutant, ECOG 2, active extrahepatic, truly NED, resectable or broadly expanded disease. PP survival conditions on reaching treatment and must not replace ITT. The Results recurrence denominator is 26/36; Figure 3 caption says 28 recurrences, consistent with a broader all-grafted report, so do not mix these denominators. QoL collection had only 55/74 per-protocol baseline questionnaires and is descriptive, not proof of a large QoL gain. Priority allocation and rapid access were part of the treatment strategy.
studies.locator: Lancet 2024;404:1107–1118. PDF pp.2–4 eligibility/committee; pp.5–6 trial flow/Table 1; pp.8–9 recurrence, safety, retransplantation, Figure 3; p.10 QoL/limitations.

studies.results: Simulation compared observed 2013 deaths/removals 93 (7%) and 4,581 patient-years with modeled TBS outcomes 48 (4%) and 5,262 patient-years. shared.proposal: Do not relax donor criteria; fund independent follow-up and pause after a serious sentinel donor event.
rules: Proposed readiness requirements: independent donor evaluation/advocacy, documented freedom to withdraw, recipient-benefit uncertainty consent, and funded medical, psychological, recovery and financial follow-up before investigational LDLT.

Proposed local follow-up: baseline, six weeks, six months, one year, two years, then annually through five years. Meet current OPTN reporting duties separately; this five-year support plan is not claimed to be a national reporting requirement.

One donor death, life-threatening complication, permanent major disability or liver failure requiring transplantation triggers an immediate pause of the relevant investigational LDLT activity and independent review. Other serious donor harm also warrants review; reopening needs independent authorization.
shared.tests: Graft/resection-specific and center-specific risk; donor recovery/employment baseline; independent consent and advocate records; funded follow-up/support; sentinel-event response owner.
shared.allocation: LDLT clearance is separate from recipient selection; the potential need for retransplantation must be included in organ-use discussions.
shared.rationale: Donor mortality is low but not zero; complication, recovery and financial burdens are more frequent. Registry missingness and selected healthy donors limit reassurance. Consent must include uncertain recipient benefit, recurrence and possible early graft loss, without pressure to proceed or relax donor criteria.
shared.counter: Older A2ALL complication rates and modern SRTR mortality are different outcomes from overlapping eras/cohorts; do not pool them. Five-year support is a reasonable local response to late morbidity, not a proven optimal schedule. Social vulnerability should trigger assistance, not categorical exclusion.
shared.certainty: Moderate certainty for the existence of material donor burden; lower certainty for individual risk and long-term recovery because of incomplete follow-up. No oncology-specific randomized donor-safety comparison.
threshold_basis: Baseline/6 weeks/6 months/1/2 years then annually to five: proposed support schedule; current mandatory reporting remains separately checked.
One sentinel event: conservative review/pause trigger, not a statistically estimated harm boundary.
No relaxed donor criteria: protection against shifting uncertain recipient benefit onto a healthy person.

shared.proposal: Use a small staged pilot with all-screened accounting and explicit safety pauses; no automatic expansion on favorable recipient survival.
rules: Proposed initial cap: ten transplants per separately approved biological stratum. Review after the first five have 90-day follow-up; no expansion decision until all first ten have at least 12-month follow-up. Reconcile vital status, graft events and known serious harms for every participant; require ≥90% completeness for other prespecified key outcomes.

In an initial experimental cohort, one all-cause recipient death, graft loss or retransplantation within 90 days triggers a pause of further experimental enrollment/transplantation pending independent review. A later possibly treatment-related death/graft loss or a donor sentinel event also triggers review/pause. Rescue care is never withheld; reopening requires independent authorization.

These are proposed conservative review triggers, not statistically validated efficacy/futility boundaries. Before opening, biostatistics and the independent board must ratify or replace them with indication-specific rules, denominators, pause authority and reopening criteria.

Capture every screened candidate, including nonrecipients, conversion to resection, dropout, deaths and access barriers; report survival from entry and from LT, recurrence, graft use, donor recovery and quality of life. Ten survivors alone do not establish benefit or authorize expansion.
shared.tests: Locked eligibility strata; prospective entry/time-zero dataset; modern comparator; adverse-event definitions; follow-up-completeness report; independently signed statistical and safety plan.
shared.allocation: Study monitoring never changes exception criteria or guarantees future access. Audit access by referral, geography, resources and donor availability without turning protected characteristics into exclusion rules.
shared.rationale: A small pilot can test feasibility, staging fidelity, data capture and acute safety, not prove durable survival benefit. Define time zero, all-screened enrollment, waitlist failures, post-LT survival/recurrence, competing death, all grafts, donor harms and patient-reported outcomes before opening. An independent board needs actual pause/reopening authority.
shared.counter: Zero observed events among ten fully followed independent patients still has a one-sided exact 95% binomial upper bound of 25.9% (1−0.05^(1/10)). Thus ten survivors cannot establish a <5% event risk. Ninety percent data completeness permits one missing patient; safety events and vital status require active ascertainment, not tolerance of unaccounted loss.
shared.certainty: Strong methodological rationale for predefinition and ITT accounting; no empirical validation of our exact cap/interim/completeness thresholds. Late recurrence demands multi-year follow-up.
threshold_basis: Ten per stratum and interim after five at 90 days: local feasibility cap and safety review cadence.
Twelve-month minimum: earliest expansion discussion, not proof of long-term cancer benefit.
≥90%: proposed non-vital key-measure completeness threshold; not permission to ignore deaths/graft events or unknown status.
One early death/graft loss/re-LT: review/pause trigger, not automatic futility or withholding rescue.
